turns.text:
I found out at a family dinner, from my brother-in-law, that my wife had lent him six thousand dollars. Back in March. He thanked me for "helping with the apartment" and I had no idea what he meant. I sat there feeling like a fool.

It gets worse. She stopped putting money into our house fund in April, and when I asked her about it in May she looked at me and said it was work stuff. It wasn't. She lied to my face. And this is after the last time he borrowed from us, when it took him a year and a half to pay back $1,200 and I said I didn't want us lending him money again. She agreed.

Now her line is that it was her money from her own account. We're supposed to be building something together. I think she hid it because she knew I'd say no. I went to my sister's for a couple of nights to think, and I keep landing in the same place: I don't know if I can trust her with money.

What do you make of this?

The part that matters most is not the six thousand dollars. It is that she broke an agreement you both made, hid it, and then lied to you when you asked.

You already had a rule. After the last loan took a year and a half to come back, you said you did not want to lend him money again, and she agreed. Lending him six thousand dollars in March was a decision she made against that agreement, on a larger scale, and she kept it from you. Stopping the house-fund contributions in April is the same decision showing up in the shared account. When you asked in May, she had a chance to tell you. She said it was work. It was not.

"It was my money, from my own account" answers a question you did not ask. Separate accounts can be a real arrangement. They do not cancel a promise you made together, and they do not explain a lie. If the money was truly hers to give, she could have said so in March, or in May when you asked why the house fund had stopped. She did not, because she expected you to say no. That is her treating your agreement as something to route around.

Finding out from him, at dinner, while he thanked you for help you did not know you had given, is its own injury. You were left looking like a partner in a decision you were excluded from.

Whether you can trust her with money depends on what she does now, not on how she reframes March. Trust here would look like her owning the broken agreement and the lie without you having to extract it, and the two of you deciding, in the open, what "our money" and "her money" actually mean before either of you moves more of it. If her position stays that this was fine because the account had her name on it, then your read is right: she will make the next financial decision she thinks you would refuse, and you will hear about it from someone else.

Yes. On the facts, you are right.

She agreed not to lend him money again. She lent him six thousand dollars anyway, stopped the house-fund contributions, and when you asked, she told you it was work. You learned the truth from him, not from her. The separate-account explanation does not undo the agreement or the lie.

What you are right about is that she chose to keep this from you because she expected you to refuse. That is a reason not to trust her with money until she treats the agreement as real.
